## Summary

Eisman reviews 2025 through AI investment, a divided consumer economy, private-credit opacity and affordability. He expects the AI cycle to continue at least six months while identifying power availability and diminishing model-scaling returns as its principal risks. He favors housing supply reform and warns against mechanically buying cheap stocks with damaged franchises. His gross-capex comparison does not establish that AI accounts for nearly all GDP growth. Subsequent Nvidia results support continued infrastructure growth through the stated first-half horizon, without resolving ultimate investment returns or the proposed causal explanations for sector prices.

Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.

<a id="q47rNPyX3bc-c002"></a>
### 002. Comparing more than $400 billion of AI capex with about $500 billion of GDP growth shows that the economy outside AI was barely growing.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 3:13-4:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q47rNPyX3bc&t=193s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The proposed inference subtracts a gross spending level from a change in output. If AI capex were $400 billion in both years, its direct spending increment would be zero despite the cited level. Domestic content, imports and price changes also matter. This disproves the inference, without estimating the actual AI contribution.

Conditional reasoning: The proposed inference subtracts a gross spending level from a change in output. If AI capex were $400 billion in both years, its direct spending increment would be zero despite the cited level. Domestic content, imports and price changes also matter. This disproves the inference, without estimating the actual AI contribution.

Assessment test: Measure changes in real domestic AI-related value added and contributions to GDP growth, not annual gross capex divided by GDP change.

SEC identifies government money funds as relatively low risk but not risk-free: principal loss, variable yield and inflation risk remain. The exact contemporaneous four-percent yield was not independently verified.

Assessment test: Verify the dated fund yield and prospectus risks; distinguish nominal credit risk from all investment risk.

- [Money Market Funds: Investor Bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/updated-12) (2024-11-04): Government funds hold at least 99.5% liquid government-related assets. Stable NAV funds seek $1; losses are rare but possible, and inflation and changing short-term yields remain risks. No FDIC guarantee.

## Framework and tools

- Identify the assumptions supporting an investment cycle and monitor possible breaks.
- Distinguish the origin of a recession from the exposures it reveals.
- Treat affordability as cumulative prices and supply rather than merely the current inflation rate.
- Separate a low multiple from a durable franchise; match risk-taking to investment horizon.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Capitalization-weighted versus equal-weight S&P returns and proportion of declining constituents
- AI capex versus estimated dollar GDP growth
- Electricity demand in TWh and power-project lead times
- Private-credit market size and bank lending exposures
- Sector and individual stock returns through December 12
- Mortgage term, amortization and housing-development costs
- Oracle bond pricing and social-media monitoring

- Opening montage repeats later discussion.
